english: Is it okay to talk (on the phone) right now?
usage: Is now a good time to talk?
the standard polite opener AFTER you placed the call and they picked up
Are you free to talk right now?
지금 = right now; pins the timing so they know you mean this moment
Do you have a minute to talk?
잠깐 (briefly) shrinks the ask and makes it easy to say yes
반말 해체; only with close friends/younger people
examples: 여보세요? 지금 통화 괜찮으세요?
Hello? Is now a good time to talk?
the bare minimum polite call opener — 여보세요 then the check
바쁘신데 죄송해요. 잠깐 통화 괜찮으세요?
Sorry to bother you when you're busy. Do you have a minute?
lead with 죄송해요 to soften before the request
야, 통화 괜찮아? 할 말 있어.
Hey, can you talk? I've got something to say.
반말 between close friends; note no -세요
nuance: This is the reflexive courtesy line the CALLER says the instant the other person answers — you confirm they can actually talk before diving in, the way an English speaker says 'Is this a good time?' 통화(通話) is Sino-Korean, literally 通 'pass/connect' + 話 'speech', i.e. 'a connected conversation', and it always means a phone/voice call — never use it for chatting face-to-face, which is just 얘기/대화. 괜찮으세요? is the all-purpose honorific 'is it okay?'; it scales down to 괜찮아? only with intimates. The big English-speaker pitfall is direction: the person who PICKED UP does not ask this — only the one who dialed does — so don't say it after you answer a call. A second trap is dropping the honorific with a boss or client; 괜찮아? to a 부장님 sounds startlingly familiar, so default to 괜찮으세요?. The nearest rival phrase, 지금 시간 괜찮으세요? ('do you have time now?'), is more general and works off the phone too, whereas 통화 괜찮으세요? specifically asks about THIS call.

Using 괜찮아? with a boss or client. It is 반말 and sounds too familiar with anyone you'd 존댓말 — the honorific 괜찮으세요? (괜찮- + 으시- + 어요) is the safe default.
Saying 통화 to mean an in-person chat. 통화 is strictly a phone call; a face-to-face conversation is 대화 or just 얘기 — '얘기 좀 괜찮아요?' for talking in person.

english: Please hold (don't hang up), and wait a moment
usage: Please don't hang up and hold on
full polite form said to a caller you've put on hold
Please stay on the line for a moment
끊지 마시고 inserts honorific -시-; the extra-polite call-center grade
shorter and brisk; 잠깐만요 = 'just a sec'
반말 to a friend; note 주세요 is gone
examples: 담당자 확인해 드릴게요. 끊지 말고 기다려 주세요.
I'll check with the person in charge. Please hold.
service line; -아 드릴게요 = doing the favor for you
잠시만 기다려 주세요. 바로 연결해 드리겠습니다.
Please hold a moment; I'll connect you right away.
formal -겠습니다 raises the politeness one more notch
엄마한테 물어볼게. 끊지 말고 기다려.
I'll ask Mom. Don't hang up, hold on.
casual, at home — plain 기다려
nuance: This is what the person holding the receiver says when they must step away briefly but want you to stay on the line — the Korean equivalent of 'please hold.' The grammar stacks two ideas: 끊다 literally means 'to cut/sever,' which is exactly how Korean conceives of hanging up (you 'cut' the call), and -지 말고 ('don't ~ and instead') warns you off doing it, while 기다려 주세요 ('please wait for me') uses the favor verb 주다 to make the wait a kindness you're granting. The classic English-speaker error is mixing 끊다 (hang up a call) with 끄다 (power off a device): phones are 끊어, but a TV or light is 꺼. A near-synonym hold-phrase is 잠시만 기다려 주세요 ('please wait a moment') — that one just asks you to wait, while 끊지 말고… specifically adds 'don't hang up,' so it's the right choice the moment there's a risk the caller gives up and ends the call. Note that to a customer you must keep 주세요; bare 끊지 말고 기다려 sounds like a barked order.

english: Shall I take a message (for them)?
usage: Would you like me to leave a message?
humble offer to write down a message for the absent person
Is there anything you'd like me to pass on?
Would you like to leave a message?
-시겠어요 puts the choice politely on the caller
Want me to leave them a message?
examples: 지금 자리에 안 계세요. 메모 남겨 드릴까요?
They're not at their desk right now. Shall I take a message?
자리에 안 계세요 = honorific 'not at their seat'
회의 중이신데, 메모 남겨 드릴까요?
They're in a meeting — would you like to leave a message?
-신데 = honorific soft lead-in giving the reason
형 지금 없는데, 메모 남겨 줄까?
Bro's not here — want me to pass on a message?
casual at home; 줄까 instead of 드릴까요
nuance: Said by whoever answers when the person the caller wants is unavailable, offering to write the message down. The engine is 드리다, the humble verb meaning 'to give / do for' a person you raise, so 남겨 드릴까요? politely volunteers to do you the favor of taking a note — by contrast, 남겨 줄까? (with plain 주다) is the casual version you'd use at home. Note 메모 here is from English 'memo' but in Korean it specifically means a short written message/note, not a corporate memorandum; 메시지 남기다 ('leave a message') is an equally natural near-synonym. The verb is 남기다 ('to leave behind'), and the conjugation trips people up: 남기- + -어 contracts to 남겨, so it's 남겨 (not 남겨다 or 남기어). The main English-speaker pitfall is register: offering 남겨 줄까요? to a customer feels a touch too plain — the humble 드릴까요? matches the service situation, since you're doing the favor for both the caller and the absent party.

usage: agent transferring your call to another line — humble -아 드릴게요
I'll connect you to the right department
담당 부서 = 'department in charge'; -로 marks the destination
formal -겠습니다 grade heard in call centers
반말, e.g. patching a friend through
examples: 기술 지원팀으로 연결해 드릴게요. 잠시만요.
I'll connect you to tech support. One moment.
-팀으로 marks the target team; 잠시만요 buys the pause
제가 처리할 수 없는 건이라, 담당자에게 연결해 드릴게요.
I can't handle this, so I'll transfer you to the right person.
-라 gives the reason for escalating
아, 그건 누나가 알아. 연결해 줄게.
Oh, my sister knows that. I'll put her on.
casual hand-off; plain 줄게
nuance: This is the agent's phrase for transferring your call to another extension or department. 연결(連結) is Sino-Korean, 連 'join' + 結 'tie', literally 'join-and-bind,' i.e. to link two points — so it fits a technical call transfer between lines. -아 드리다 again uses humble 드리다, making it a polite promise to do the routing for you; the most formal centers escalate to 연결해 드리겠습니다, while 연결해 줄게 works casually. The crucial near-synonym contrast English speakers must master is 연결 vs 연락: 연결 ('connect') is wiring two parties together in the moment (transfer the call), whereas 연락(連絡) ('get in touch / contact') is reaching out to someone later — '나중에 연락드릴게요' is 'I'll contact you later,' and you cannot swap in 연결 there. A second contrast is 연결 vs 바꾸다: 연결 is a system transfer to another line/department, while 바꿔 드릴게요 is simply handing the same phone to a person nearby. The common error is the redundant causative 연결시켜 드릴게요 — plain 연결해 already means 'connect (for you),' so 시키다 is unnecessary.

english: They're not available / not in (missed call)
usage: plain polite statement that someone is away
fixed compound noun — the label your phone screen shows
honorific -세요 when the absent person outranks you
examples: 부장님 지금 부재중이세요. 메모 남겨 드릴까요?
The manager is out right now. Shall I take a message?
office phone; 부재중이세요 raises the boss
부재중 전화가 세 통이나 와 있네.
Whoa, I've got three missed calls.
통 = counter for calls; -이나 conveys 'as many as'
담당자가 부재중입니다. 잠시 후 다시 연락드리겠습니다.
The agent is unavailable. We'll contact you again shortly.
formal -입니다 service announcement
nuance: A semi-formal word meaning 'absent / away from one's seat,' used both to explain that someone can't come to the phone and, as the set noun 부재중 전화, to label a missed call on your screen. The 한자 makes the register: 부재(不在) is 不 'not' + 在 'be present / exist,' literally 'not-present,' plus 중(中) 'in the middle of' — so 부재중 is 'in a state of being absent,' which sounds officeworthy and official, distinctly more buttoned-up than the everyday 없어요 ('isn't here'). That is the key synonym contrast: with a friend who just stepped out you'd say 잠깐 나갔어요 ('stepped out for a bit') or 자리 비웠어요, never the stiff 부재중이에요. English speakers also slip on 부재중 vs 통화 중: 부재중 means they're AWAY from the phone, while 통화 중 means they're THERE but already on another call — opposite situations. Note the honorific split: about a respected person it's 부재중이세요, but about a line or yourself you keep plain 부재중이에요.

english: I'll get in touch with you later
usage: humble promise to reach back out; -드릴게요 raises the listener
I'll reach out in a bit
이따가 = later TODAY (not 나중에, which can be open-ended)
I will get back to you
examples: 지금 좀 바빠서요. 나중에 연락드릴게요.
I'm a bit busy right now. I'll contact you later.
-아서요 trails off to soften the reason for ending
확인하고 나중에 연락드릴게요.
I'll check and get back to you later.
-고 chains 'check, then contact'
나 지금 운전 중이야. 나중에 연락할게.
I'm driving right now. I'll call you later.
casual; 운전 중 = mid-driving
nuance: The polite way to wrap up or postpone a conversation by promising to reach out again — it works to end a call gracefully or to defer a decision. 연락(連絡) is Sino-Korean, 連 'connect' + 絡 'tie/wrap,' literally 'connecting threads,' and crucially it means 'contact' in general: a call, a text, or a message all count, so don't read it as 'phone call' specifically. The honorific engine is 드리다, the humble 'do for you' verb, which raises the listener — with friends it relaxes to 연락할게. Two contrasts English speakers need: first, 연락 (get in touch later) vs 연결 (transfer a call right now) — never interchangeable; saying 연결드릴게요 to mean 'I'll contact you' is wrong. Second, the timing word: 나중에 means 'later' open-endedly (could be tomorrow), while 이따가 means 'a bit later today,' so promising 나중에 연락드릴게요 commits you to less than 이따가. One register caution: 드리다 raises whoever you're speaking to, so using 연락드릴게요 toward someone clearly junior to you can sound oddly over-deferential — plain 연락할게요 fits better there.

english: I'll put them on / pass you over (to another person)
usage: I'll put them on the line
humble; handing the SAME phone to the person you want
One moment, I'll pass you over
잠시만요 buys the beat while you fetch them
I'll put the person in charge on
examples: 사장님 찾으세요? 잠시만요, 바꿔 드릴게요.
Looking for the boss? One moment, I'll put them on.
찾으세요 = honorific 'are you looking for'
제가 잘 몰라서요. 아는 사람으로 바꿔 드릴게요.
I'm not sure, so I'll put on someone who knows.
-으로 marks who you're swapping TO
엄마 찾아? 잠깐만, 바꿔 줄게.
Looking for Mom? Hold on, I'll put her on.
casual at home; 줄게 not 드릴게요
nuance: Used when the person who answered hands the receiver to whoever the caller actually wanted to reach. The verb is 바꾸다, literally 'to change / swap,' and on the phone it idiomatically means 'swap who is speaking' — so you're not 'changing' anything physical, you're exchanging the voice on the line. -아 드리다 (humble 드리다) makes it a polite favor; 바꿔 줄게 is the home/peer version. The single most useful contrast here is 바꾸다 vs 연결하다: 바꿔 드릴게요 is for handing over the SAME phone to a person right next to you (a family member, a colleague in the room), whereas 연결해 드릴게요 is a technical TRANSFER to another line or department. Use the wrong one and it sounds off — saying 연결해 드릴게요 at home to pass the phone to your mom is comically corporate. The conjugation also trips learners: the stem is 바꾸- and 바꾸- + -어 contracts to 바꿔 (not 바껴, which would come from a non-existent 바끼다).

usage: polite, said TO the caller; 거셨어요 = honorific past of 걸다
I think you have the wrong number
-것 같다 hedges so you don't sound blunt
There's no one by that name here
the usual follow-up; -는데요 trails off softly
반말 — typically the CALLER admitting it
examples: 김철수요? 전화 잘못 거셨어요. 그런 사람 없는데요.
Kim Chul-su? You've got the wrong number — no one by that name here.
name + 요? echoes back what they asked
죄송하지만 전화 잘못 거신 것 같은데요.
Sorry, but I think you've dialed the wrong number.
죄송하지만 cushions before correcting them
어? 미안, 내가 전화 잘못 걸었어.
Huh? Sorry, I dialed the wrong number.
the caller owning the mistake; 내가 + 걸었어
nuance: What you say when someone reaches you by mistake. The verb is 걸다, the standard word for placing a call (전화를 걸다, literally 'hang/put up a call'), and here it appears as the honorific past 거셨어요, so you're politely telling the CALLER that they dialed wrong — note you raise them with -시- even while correcting them. Flip the subject and the caller admits it as 제가 잘못 걸었어요 ('I misdialed'), so who 'owns' the error decides the wording: 거셨어요 (you) vs 걸었어요 (I). The headline English-speaker pitfall is the irregular conjugation: 걸다 is a ㄹ-stem verb, so before -시- the ㄹ drops — the honorific is 거시- → 거셨어요, NOT the over-regular 걸으셨어요. A second contrast is 걸다 (place a call) vs 받다 (receive/answer a call): you 전화를 걸다 to dial out and 전화를 받다 to pick up, so 'wrong number' attaches to 걸다, the dialing action. To soften the correction, Koreans love padding it: 잘못 거신 것 같은데요 ('seems you may have the wrong number').

english: Please call back in a little while
usage: asks the caller to retry later rather than wait on hold
Call back in a bit, please
조금 이따 = casual 'in a little bit'
examples: 지금 회의 중이라, 잠시 후에 다시 걸어 주세요.
I'm in a meeting now, so please call back in a little while.
-이라 gives the reason; 회의 중 = mid-meeting
통화량이 많습니다. 잠시 후에 다시 걸어 주세요.
Call volume is high. Please call again shortly.
the exact automated message you hear when lines are busy
나 밥 먹고 있어. 이따 다시 걸어.
I'm eating. Call me back later.
casual; -고 있어 = in the middle of, 이따 = later today
nuance: A polite way to ask the caller to try again soon instead of holding the line. It breaks into 잠시 후에 ('after a short while': 잠시 from 한자 暫時 'brief time,' + 후 後 'after') and 다시 걸어 주세요 ('please dial again'), where 걸다 is the verb for placing a call and 주세요 frames the redial as a favor you're requesting. This is famously the wording in automated busy-line announcements, so it doubles as a system prompt you'll recognize. Two pitfalls for English speakers: first, the voice — 'call back' is the ACTIVE 걸다 → 걸어 주세요, not the passive 걸리다; 다시 걸려 주세요 is wrong because 걸리다 means 'to be caught/take time,' not 'to dial.' Second, don't confuse 잠시 후에 ('after a moment,' a future time when you should ACT) with 잠시만요 ('hold on a sec,' said to freeze someone in the present) — different functions: one sends the caller away to retry, the other keeps them put. A natural near-synonym is 이따 다시 전화 주세요 ('phone again later'), slightly more colloquial than the formal 잠시 후에.

english: The signal is weak / poor reception
usage: states the reception problem; 신호 takes -가 as subject
It's because reception is weak here
-아서요 trails off, giving the reason a call dropped
I can't get a good signal
잡히다 = the signal is 'caught'/picked up; very natural alt
examples: 여보세요? 여기 신호가 약해서 잘 안 들려요.
Hello? Reception's weak here so I can't hear well.
links cause (-아서) to effect (안 들려요)
지하라서 신호가 약해요. 끊고 다시 걸게요.
I'm underground so the signal's weak. Let me hang up and call back.
-라서 reason; proposes 끊고 다시 = hang up then redial
산속이라 신호 약해. 이따 통화하자.
I'm in the mountains, signal's weak. Let's talk later.
casual; -자 = let's; 통화하자 = let's talk (by phone)
nuance: The natural way to explain why a call sounds garbled or keeps dropping: the cellular 신호 is 약하다 ('weak'). 신호(信號) is Sino-Korean, 信 'trust/sign' + 號 'mark/signal,' literally a 'sign-mark,' and it covers signals broadly — also a traffic 신호(등) ('traffic light') — so context tells you it's reception. A frequent English-speaker trap is reaching for the loanword 사인 (sign) for 'signal'; on a phone the word is 신호, while 사인 in Korean usually means a 'signature' or a hand 'sign,' not cell reception. The other classic error is the adjective: signal strength is 약하다/세다 ('weak/strong'), NOT 작다/크다 ('small/big') — 신호가 작아요 sounds wrong the way 'the signal is small' does in English. A very common near-synonym is 신호가 잘 안 잡혀요 ('the signal doesn't get picked up well'), built on 잡히다 ('be caught'); Koreans use it interchangeably with 약해요. Pair any of these with 잘 안 들려요 ('I can't hear well') to connect the weak signal to the reason you keep saying 'what?'.

usage: Can you hear me all right?
honorific check on the OTHER side mid-call; subject is them
Can you hear my voice clearly?
제 목소리 spells out exactly what they should be hearing
지금은 = 'now (as opposed to before)'; after fixing reception
examples: 여보세요? 제 목소리 잘 들리세요?
Hello? Can you hear my voice okay?
opening check when the audio sounds shaky
여기로 옮겼는데 지금은 잘 들리세요?
I moved over here — is it clear now?
-는데 sets up the change before re-checking
야, 잘 들려? 자꾸 끊기는 것 같은데.
Hey, can you hear me? It keeps cutting out.
casual; 끊기다 = (the call) keeps dropping
nuance: The flip side of reporting 잘 안 들려요 ('I can't hear well'): instead of describing your own trouble, you ask whether the OTHER person can hear YOU, which is why it's phrased about them. The key grammar is voice: 들리다 is the intransitive/passive 'to be heard / be audible' (something reaches the ear on its own), so 잘 들리세요? literally asks 'does it come through to you well?' — the honorific -세요 raises the listener. English speakers must not confuse this with 듣다, the transitive 'to listen' that takes an object: asking 잘 듣고 있어요? means 'are you listening (paying attention)?', which sounds like you're scolding them, not checking reception — so the reception check is 들리세요?, never 듣다. A second look-alike trap is 들리다 (be audible) vs 들다 (to lift/hold, or 'cost/enter'): totally different verbs that only resemble each other on paper. Natural partners are 잘 (well) and 안 (not): 잘 들려요 / 잘 안 들려요 / 안 들려요. On video calls the same 들리세요? is the universal audio check.

english: They're on another call right now
usage: They're on the phone right now
honorific -세요 about the person the caller wants
The line's busy / on a call
plain polite, about a line or neutral subject
I'm on the phone right now
examples: 부장님 지금 통화 중이세요. 잠시 후에 다시 걸어 주세요.
The manager's on another call. Please call back shortly.
통화 중이세요 raises the boss; pairs with a redial request
몇 번을 걸어도 계속 통화 중이네요.
No matter how many times I call, the line's still busy.
-아도 = 'even if'; frustrated caller noticing it
미안, 나 지금 통화 중이야. 이따 연락할게.
Sorry, I'm on the phone. I'll get back to you.
casual about YOURSELF — plain, no -세요
nuance: Explains that a person's line is occupied because they're already talking to someone else. 통화 중 = 'in the middle of a call,' where 통화(通話) is 'a connected conversation' (通 'connect' + 話 'speech') and 중(中) is the 한자 'middle/in the midst of,' so the whole thing is 'mid-call.' The honorific is the subtle part English speakers miss: add -세요 only when it's ABOUT a person you respect (부장님 통화 중이세요), but keep plain 통화 중이에요 about a line, and 통화 중이야 about yourself — never raise your own status by saying 저 통화 중이세요. The essential synonym contrast is 통화 중 vs 부재중: 통화 중 means they ARE at the phone but already speaking, whereas 부재중 means they're AWAY from it entirely — so picking the wrong one tells the caller the opposite of the truth. Note 중 is a productive suffix you'll reuse everywhere: 회의 중 (in a meeting), 식사 중 (eating), 운전 중 (driving). A natural collocation is 계속 통화 중 ('the line stays busy') when repeated calls won't get through.
